topics.topic: Unit 3 drill 5 corrected at the board, student by student, because it is part of homework 3 and she did not want it learned wrong - 'I just want to make sure I correct those, because I don't want you to learn it in the wrong way.' Seven or eight students were sent up in turn and she corrected the handwriting itself as much as the spelling: keep the extra decorative strokes the book prints out of your handwriting because they read as another letter, make the taa marbuuTa longer than its connector so the word stays readable, do not connect an initial letter on its left-hand side, and add the fatHa where the alif requires it. This is also where the KASRA-AFTER-ALIF rule surfaced, which she then repeated three more times across the hour: when a kasra sits under the letter following an alif, the alif shifts toward an e-like vowel rather than a plain long aa. She caught a student producing it correctly later and made the class say why

THE RULE OF THE HOUR, taught from scratch on the board: the THREE CASES in which waaw and yaa stop being long vowels and act as CONSONANTS (w and y). (1) At the BEGINNING of a word - either letter, not both - which is why the words for homework/duty and for must/should begin with a consonant sound. (2) When TWO VOWELS stand next to each other, the FIRST is always the consonant and the second is the vowel; she confirmed to a student that this holds for all three Arabic vowels, and that there are only three. (3) When a SUKUUN sits on the waaw or yaa, most often mid-word - this is what separates the word for house from a word read with a long ii. Bundled with it, the unspoken tashkiil conventions that make those readable in unvocalised text: assume a fatHa at the BEGINNING of a word unless told otherwise (a few words take Damma or kasra instead) and assume a SUKUUN at the END. She also flagged a TEXTBOOK ERROR here in response to a student question: the book says waaw/yaa act as a consonant when 'preceded by or followed by' a vowel, and she says it should be FOLLOWED by only - 'probably there is a mistake there. I didn't pay attention to that one, actually'

Applying the rule out loud, around the room, for nearly half the class - listening exercises 5, 6, 7 and 8 and drills 7 and 8 from unit 3, pages 53-57. Each student read one word and she diagnosed it against the three cases rather than just correcting it: the word for dialogue (kasra under the Haa, then waaw as consonant), the word for houses (yaa and waaw adjacent, so the yaa is the consonant), the word for a long robe worn by men in the Gulf as well as by women, the word for pair or husband, the word for good with a sukuun on the yaa, the word for between. Two of the drills she worked here - 7 and 8 - are drills she has ASSIGNED as part of homework 4, so that portion is already corrected. Her closing summary of the block was a promise about consistency: 'it's getting harder now. You know more letters and it's confusing. The yeah and the wow, I know they're confusing. So just try to remember the rules, the rules that we give. The good thing is they're consistent'

The new unit 3 vocabulary list, introduced spoken rather than written, explicitly so that Thursday can be a speaking class. She traded drill 9 (which she did with her other sections) for this. Words taught with pronunciation drilled aloud: wa (and - always written attached to the following word, never spaced, so you have to recognise it as a separate word), Hijaab, bayt (house/home) and bayti (my home - the possessive yaa suffix, which she then drilled on every noun), shaari3 / shaari3i (street), waajib / waajibi (homework or duty), akhbaar (news - she corrected the class hard on akh- rather than ak-, since akbar means greatest), kitaab plus kitaabuka and kitaabuki (your book, masculine and feminine, in fuSHa, with the Shami forms as well), Habiibi / Habiibti (with a careful note on when it is and is not appropriate across genders), SabaaH al-khayr answered with SabaaH an-nuur (a good morning answered with an enlightened morning - and unlike marHaba you cannot simply return the same phrase), the vocative yaa (the 'O' of 'O Lord' in the Psalms), kayfa al-Haal (Haal meaning condition, not marital status), al-Hamdu lillaah with a Christian alternative al-Hamdu li-r-Rabb that she teaches as OPTIONAL and explained the reasoning for, jayyid / jayyida (good, masculine and feminine, so gendered adjectives like Spanish), bi-khayr, haadhaa / haadhihi, and laysa for negation. The 3ayn appears in 'street' before it has been formally taught, so she taught its sound informally - 'try to say ah and then try to shock yourself' - and told them to exaggerate it so they do not collapse it into a hamza

announcements.text: HOMEWORK 4 IS DUE FRIDAY 2026-09-18, and she corrected an error in it before class. 'Homework 4, let's talk about it. This is not until Friday. So there was some duplication on this one. I corrected it. Thank you, Sydney, for letting me know.' The contents as she read them: DICTATION drills 7, 8 and 11; drill 10, which is a letter-connection exercise of the same kind as unit 2 drill 13; and drills 12 and 14 answered ON LINGCO. The instruction she stressed: where a drill says to listen, the audio is on Lingco but you do NOT submit there - you listen in order to place the tashkiil on the written words. 'Read the instruction. If they say listen to it, that means there is a part on lingo, you just need to listen, not submit on lingo.' Her pacing advice: 'start early, don't wait until Friday. Sometimes sitting like one time over the homework is just too annoying, so divide it two, three times is much better.'

A NEW AND SIGNIFICANT GRADING POLICY, said out loud for the first time: EXAMS CAN BE RETAKEN. 'when we come into exams, let's say you took the exam and you're not happy with your grade, you want to take, it's not going to be the same exam, but similar exam. If you want to take it again, I'll send you to the testing center, you could take it again. This show me that you're putting effort, extra effort, and it's helpful also for you because you're reviewing at least one more time. So if you want to do that, I'm happy to help you. Don't mind regrading.' A different exam of similar construction, taken at the testing centre, on request. She said the same about the oral assessment: 'If you need to repeat it, let me know. I'll give you another chance, no problem.'

THE UNIT 2 ORAL ASSESSMENT WAS DUE TONIGHT (2026-09-15) and it is GRADED AGAINST A RUBRIC, not for completion. A student asked directly and she was unambiguous: 'No, you have to do it correctly. This one is a speaking. So if you miss any part, that means I have to deduct points according to the rubric. So I look for what we talked here in class, I told you, make sure you answer this part, make sure you ask this question. So those, if they're not in the assessment, then I have to deduct that point.' She used 40 or 45 out of 50 as her example, and offered a retake to anyone who wants one.

THURSDAY 2026-09-17 IS A SPEAKING CLASS AND THE NEW VOCABULARY IS THE PREPARATION. Her last words before dismissing: 'I'll stop here. Please go over them before Thursday so we could start speaking and making sentences and having more options.' The list is the unit 3 vocabulary she introduced today, from page 61 onward. She rearranged the hour to make this possible - she did drill 9 with her other sections and skipped it here to get the vocabulary in.

SHE SKIPPED DRILL 9 WITH THIS SECTION, and said so: 'with the other classes, I did drill 9, but with you, I'm trying to introduce you to the new vocab list today so we could speak on Thursday. Okay, so you're okay with this?' Worth noting because it means this section is one drill behind the others on written work and one step ahead on speaking. Drill 9 was not assigned as homework either.

PLURALS ARE POSTPONED. Asked about the plural of bayt, she gave it but deferred the pattern: 'We'll postpone the plural until next class, until one or two. But for now, we're going to just learn singular, so you need to learn bayt, house, or home.' Learn the singulars only for now.

THE ARABIC/INTERNATIONAL EVENT THAT WAS CANCELLED LAST WEEK HAS BEEN RESCHEDULED TO THIS THURSDAY at the International Student Center, second floor, with the office door off the lobby. She joked about the late cancellation - 'that's very Arabic, so you have to get used to it' - and showed a QR code for their Instagram. The TIME IS GARBLED in the recording (it reads only 'At 30 this Thursday'), so no time can be given. There is a second event next week during Global Focus Week, where her husband is speaking, with no location or time known yet - 'once I know all the information, I'll let you know as well.' Both are optional, neither is coursework, so neither is entered as a commitment.

OFFICE HOURS ARE UNDERBOOKED AND SHE IS FLEXIBLE ABOUT THEM. She came in early today for a student who cancelled at the last minute, and repeated the offer twice in the first two minutes: 'If you have any difficulties in anything, just let me know, okay? And you can come to my office. We can check my office hours. If the office hours don't work for your schedule, let me know so we can work something else.' She also prayed specifically over a student's request for help understanding Arabic.

A CAMPUS POWER OUTAGE hit the building in the last twenty minutes of class - the lights went out and campus internet dropped, though her phone kept working off the cell tower. She checked whether the class wanted to leave and they continued in the dark. This is the same outage the Genetics class was discussing at its break the same afternoon.

TWO BOOK ERRORS NAMED IN ONE HOUR. (1) The consonant rule: the book says waaw/yaa function as consonants when 'preceded by or followed by' a vowel; she says FOLLOWED by only, and told the student who raised it that there is probably a mistake in the text. (2) A vocabulary gloss: the book translates the word she taught as 'peach', and she says that is wrong - it is PLUM, and peach is a different word entirely. She added both that word and bayt to the required vocabulary because they appear in the writing exercise.

Where a drill says listen, the Lingco audio is for hearing the tashkiil only - the answers are written out, not submitted on Lingco. Drills 7 and 8 were already corrected in class on 9/15

off_slide: The 3ayn taught by feel rather than by rule, weeks before the letter is formally introduced, because it turns up in the word for street: 'it comes from where the Haa comes from, the epiglottal muscle in here. So the funny way to make the sound is try to say ah and then try to shock yourself.' She told them to EXAGGERATE it deliberately in practice so it does not collapse into a hamza - her example being students who write and say Ali when she wants 3ali

The al-Hamdu lillaah discussion, which was the most substantial cultural teaching of the hour. She explained why the phrase saturates Arab speech (a Muslim belief that repetition earns reward) against the Christian caution about using the name in vain, and taught an alternative, al-Hamdu li-r-Rabb, as an OPTIONAL substitute she uses where it is doable. She told a story about a student who used it at the gym and was stopped by a Muslim who asked who had taught her that - 'because it's not familiar to them as Muslims, but the Christians, they use it'
That al-Hamdu lillaah on its own is already a complete answer to kayfa al-Haal - 'if you just say praise to God, that means you're good because you're praising God'
The vocative yaa explained through the Psalms - the 'O' in 'I love you, O Lord' is exactly the Arabic yaa - and through Shami usage for calling someone, especially a father
The Habiibi etiquette: same-gender use is free and casual, across genders it implies a fiancee or girlfriend, and it is normal with children, nieces, nephews - and, she added, with her dogs

SabaaH al-khayr is NOT answered by repeating it, unlike marHaba which can be returned unchanged. A student asked precisely this and she said returning it is possible but uncommon; SabaaH an-nuur is the real reply, and it means an enlightened morning in answer to a good one

Her handwriting corrections, which are not in the book: drop the decorative strokes the printed text adds because in handwriting they read as another letter, and stretch the taa marbuuTa longer than its connection so the word is readable

Why some vocabulary entries carry transliteration and others do not - a student asked, and the answer is that the ones you can already decode from the letters taught so far are left bare, and only the words containing untaught letters get the transliteration crutch

The gendered-adjective question from a student - 'is it like in Spanish where objects are feminine and masculine?' - answered yes, with jayyid / jayyida and haadhaa / haadhihi as the immediate examples
The class debating with her whether to keep going once the lights went out, and continuing
terms: waaw as consonant (w) vs long vowel (uu)
yaa as consonant (y) vs long vowel (ii)
the three Arabic long vowels (alif, waaw, yaa)

notes: THE EXAM RETAKE POLICY IS THE MOST VALUABLE THING IN THIS HOUR and it is not on any slide, in any syllabus section anyone has read, or in Canvas. If Parker is unhappy with an Arabic exam grade he can ask her and she will set a SIMILAR (not identical) exam at the testing centre. Test 1 on units 1-4 is 2026-10-13. She frames it as evidence of effort rather than as a concession, so asking costs nothing.

HOMEWORK 4 IS DUE FRIDAY 2026-09-18, which breaks the pattern - homeworks 1, 2 and 3 were all due the day after they were assigned. Two days of margin, and she asked them explicitly to split it across sittings rather than do it in one. Two of the six drills in it (7 and 8) were worked and corrected in class today, so that part is a transcription job rather than fresh work.

THE SUBMISSION MECHANICS FOR THE WRITTEN HALF WERE NOT RESTATED TODAY. The 'canvas' destination on that commitment comes from the established pattern set on 9/1 and 9/10 - photograph each drill in portrait, name the file after the drill, upload to Canvas, no HEIC. She named only the drill numbers this time. The Lingco half (drills 12 and 14) she did state explicitly.

THE ONE RULE TO DRILL BEFORE THURSDAY, because the entire second half of the class was students getting it wrong: waaw and yaa are consonants in exactly three situations - at the START of a word, as the FIRST of two adjacent vowels, and when carrying a SUKUUN. Everything else is a long vowel. Paired with the two default assumptions that make unvocalised text readable: fatHa at the beginning of a word, sukuun at the end.

SECOND: the kasra-after-alif rule, which she stated four separate times and which two students still missed. A kasra under the letter following an alif pulls the alif toward an e-like vowel. She drilled it as a question ('how did we tell about this one?') rather than as a statement, which usually means it is going to be tested.

A live correction to the textbook that should go into any card made from it: the book's condition for waaw/yaa acting as a consonant reads 'preceded by or followed by' a vowel; she says only FOLLOWED by is correct and called the book's version probably a mistake. Separately, the book glosses the plum word as 'peach' and she says that is simply wrong.

THE ARABIC IN THIS TRANSCRIPT IS SEVERELY MANGLED and no Arabic word in this record has been quoted from the caption text. Teams renders Arabic phonetically through an English model, so 'wa alaikum salam' appears as normal text but 'SabaaH an-nuur' becomes 'Sabah Hanu' and 'Sabahnur', 'jayyid' becomes 'Javed', 'shaari3' becomes 'Sarah', 'akhbaar' becomes 'Akbar' (which is a DIFFERENT WORD she stopped the class to distinguish), 'sukuun' becomes 'succoon', 'supoon' and 'so cool', 'tashkiil' becomes 'Tishkil' and 'tushki', and bayt/bayti appear as 'bait', 'beat', 'bead', 'Beiti' and 'belly'. The vocabulary list here is reconstructed from her English glosses and from the Alif Baa unit 3 list, not transliterated off the captions, and the individual drill words read aloud are mostly unrecoverable.

The event this Thursday at the International Student Center has a garbled time in the recording ('At 30 this Thursday') and is left out of commitments for that reason. It is optional and not coursework; if it matters, the group's Instagram was shown as a QR code in class.

This section is one drill behind her other sections - she skipped drill 9 here to buy time for the vocabulary. Drill 9 was not assigned, so it is not owed, but it is a gap in the written practice for this unit and worth doing on his own if the waaw/yaa rule still feels shaky.

Roughly 9 minutes correcting drill 5 at the board, 12 teaching the three-case consonant rule, 28 on read-aloud practice through listening exercises 5-8 and drills 7 and 8, and 19 on the new vocabulary, with about 7 minutes of announcements and prayer at the start. Almost nothing here exists as a slide - this is a board-and-book class, and her slides are never posted to Canvas, so the recording IS the material.
